patterns.comment: This grammar's own authoring convention, not a tf semantic: to real tf, ;/echo, ;; echo, and ; /echo are all equally just a comment, no distinction whatsoever. Here, ; (or #) immediately followed by / with no space marks a line of CODE that's been commented out, so it's still highlighted as code (dimmed like a comment, but with its commands/strings/substitutions/operators all visible) rather than as prose. ;; and ; / (space before the /) are both left as plain prose — see editors/vscode/README.md.
patterns.name: comment.line.semicolon.code.tf

patterns.comment: A line is a comment when its first non-whitespace character is ; or # (tf's own load_file() rule, not just the ;; convention test-case headers use). tfscript comments routinely ARE unlabeled example code (see this project's own test-case headers), so substitutions and operators are still highlighted inside, and so is a /word that's a REAL, known command name (#knownCommandsInProse) — but not an arbitrary /word, since a plain-English '/' (e.g. "50/50") is a much easier false positive in prose than a name that happens to exactly match one of tf's ~214 real commands. An unrecognized name (a custom macro, e.g. /my_func) only lights up on an explicit ;/ commented-code line, not in plain prose. Quoted strings are deliberately NOT nested here either: an ordinary contraction like "don't" would start a fake string looking for a closing apostrophe.
patterns.name: comment.line.semicolon.tf

continuation.comment: A trailing \ continues this line onto the next, UNLESS the character right before it is % (a literal %\ is an escaped backslash, not a continuation — see src/logicalEntries.ts's continuesToNextLine; that case is already covered by #substitutions' character-escape pattern, which this negative lookbehind steps aside for). Deliberately scoped under comment.* purely for the visual effect — a theme that mutes prose comments mutes this the same way — not a claim that a continuation marker IS a comment; no standalone punctuation.* scope reliably gets that same deemphasis.
continuation.name: constant.character.escape.line-continuation.tf

numbers.comment: Integers, decimals, and reals with an exponent (tinyfugue/htmldoc/topics/expressions.html's Operands section). Not attempting dtime (h:m:s) or atime forms here — those are ordinary-looking numbers with colons, too easy to confuse with other uses of ':' in a cosmetic grammar.
numbers.name: constant.numeric.tf

substitutions.comment: tf's full substitution grammar — htmldoc/topics/substitution.html covers %selector, %{...}, %;, %|, $[...], $(...), and ${...}/$name all as ONE topic, 'substitution', which is also how a tf scripter actually thinks of them: all sigils that mean 'something gets replaced here before this runs'. Every sigil capture below therefore carries two scopes together — punctuation.definition.substitution.tf (the shared family, so a theme that only wants to flag 'this is a substitution marker' can do that for every one of them with a single rule) plus a specific second scope for which KIND: punctuation.definition.variable.tf (%, a real dereference), .expression.tf ($[...]), .command.tf ($(...)), or .macro.tf (${...}/$name — substituting another macro's BODY, not a variable). %;/%|'s % carries only the family scope, no second one, since separating commands isn't dereferencing anything. Brackets get their own punctuation.section.bracket.* scope too, same convention VS Code's own bundled bash grammar uses for ${...} (confirmed by reading shell-unix-bash.tmLanguage.json directly). None of this is picked for how it happens to render in any one theme — whether a theme colors punctuation.definition.* or punctuation.section.bracket.* at all is that theme's own call, not something this grammar chases.

patterns.comment: %{selector} / %{selector-default} — braced variable, argument, or %P/%L/%R substitution. The inner content is matched twice over: first the common case (a bare selector, highlighted as a plain name/reference) via #substitutionSelector, then anything left over (a '-default' tail, which htmldoc/topics/substitution.html says may itself contain variable/macro/expression/command substitutions) falls through to the fully recursive set. The (?<!%) guards against %%{ — percent compression (two %'s collapsing to one literal %) — being misread as a live %{ opener; without it, a found-in-the-wild %%{...} (tinyfugue/lib/tf/kbstack.tf) would open a begin/end region at the wrong %, hunting for a '}' match that can swallow far more than intended.

Unbraced %selector, exactly matching htmldoc/topics/substitution.html's documented list (verified directly — an earlier version of this pattern invented a nonexistent '1-5'-style range form, which caused a real false positive elsewhere once checked against real-world scripts; there is no range form in tf's selector grammar at all): a name, #, ?, *, a plain positional number, -N (all except the first N), L/LN (last/Nth-last; bare 'L' means 'L1'), -L/-LN, or P/PN/R (all just names shape-wise). No brackets to decompose here, so sigil + selector share one combined match.

%; separates commands on one logical line; %| does too, and also pipes the first command's output into the second. The % is the same sigil color as every other %, consistently — only the ;/| itself gets the operator color, since that's the part that's actually punctuation/control flow.
%%... — percent compression: one fewer %, used to write a literal % (e.g. %% for one %).
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.tf

patterns.comment: $[expression] — a redundant-inside-/if/elseif/while expression substitution (dollar-bracket-in-if); legal anywhere an expression is read. Fully recursive inside: real operators, numbers, functions, strings, and further substitutions all apply, same as any other expression context.

$(command) — command substitution: command runs as a macro body and its echoed output is substituted in place. Fully recursive inside, but with command-context patterns (a real tf command, not a bare expression).
$$... — dollar compression: one fewer $, used to write a literal $ (e.g. $$ for one $).
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.tf

patterns.comment: ${name} or bare $name — macro substitution: the body of macro `name` is substituted in place.
\n (decimal/octal/0x hex character code) or \c (escaped literal character) — tf's character substitution, same %{backslash} mechanism as a shell's backslash escapes.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.tf

patterns.comment: Bare {selector} / {selector-default} — tinyfugue/htmldoc/topics/expressions.html: "in expressions, it is easiest to omit the % and just use the {selector[-default]} part". Same pairing as %{...} above, minus the sigil (there isn't one). Deliberately also matches tinyfugue/htmldoc/topics/patterns.html's OTHER use of {...} — glob-pattern word alternation, e.g. {storm|chup*} — which is a different construct entirely; a regex grammar can't tell "this {...} is an expression selector" from "this {...} is a glob group" apart without knowing which argument position expects which, so both get the same treatment. Not wrong exactly either way — both are "a block with content" — just not always literally what it is.

substitutionSelector.comment: The common case inside %{...}: a bare selector with no '-default' tail. Same shape as the unbraced %selector match above, minus the %. Deliberately ambiguous with a '1-foofle' range-vs-default split the same way the unbraced form already is (see that pattern's own note) — not re-solving a pre-existing heuristic limitation here. No anchor needed: tried first in the enclosing begin/end region's patterns, so it's already attempted starting right where scanning resumed (immediately after the opening brace) before any of the recursive fallbacks below get a turn.
substitutionSelector.name: variable.parameter.tf

functions.comment: tf's documented built-in expression functions: tinyfugue/htmldoc/topics/functions.html's own anchors (85 names) plus the handful of commands htmldoc/commands/*.html separately documents as also callable as a function — addworld, echo, escape, eval, ftime, prompt, replace, send, substitute, textencode (replace is in both lists). Anything else shaped like name( — a macro called as a function, or a builtin command called as a function, both real per functions.html's own resolution order ("builtin function, then macro, then builtin command") — falls through to the unrecognized-name pattern below (entity.name.function.tf), same known/unrecognized split as #commands and the same support.*-vs-entity.name.* convention, since this engine has no way to confirm an arbitrary macro name without the project's own case harness.

patterns.comment: Unrecognized name immediately followed by ( — presumably your own macro, called as a function. Same color as an unrecognized /command (#commands' #unknownCommand), since both mean the same thing: "a name this engine can't confirm, probably yours."
patterns.name: entity.name.function.tf

knownCommandsInProse.comment: The real, complete list of tf command names (keyword table + builtin dispatch table + stdlib.tf macros) this project's own LSP server already extracts for completion — src/data/commands.ts's ALL_COMMANDS, deduped and lowercased. Regenerate with (from the repo root, after `npm run build`): node -e "const {ALL_COMMANDS}=require('./dist/data/commands'); console.log([...new Set(ALL_COMMANDS.map(c=>c.name.toLowerCase()))].sort().join('|'))" — 214 names as of tinyfugue's current tree; the exact same list also appears in #commands' known-command branch, so update both together. support.function.tf: tf provides this command, same as a known #functions call. Deliberately only used inside plain-prose comments (see #comments); real code and ;/-marked commented code use #commands instead, since there every /word, known or custom, is a real command and gets the known/unrecognized scope split either way.
knownCommandsInProse.name: support.function.tf

operators.comment: tinyfugue/htmldoc/topics/expressions.html's full operator table — valid inside $[...], /if, /elseif, /while, and /def -E conditions. Highlighted wherever it appears (not scoped to just those contexts, same tradeoff the #commands rule already makes): no modulo/bitwise operators exist in tf (mod() is a function, and % is reserved entirely for substitution — see #substitutions), and bare / is deliberately excluded here even though division is real, since it would conflict visually with the far more common /command prefix.
operators.name: keyword.operator.tf

commands.comment: A top-level /word: tf's control-flow keywords, C builtins, and stdlib.tf macros are all written the same way, plus a user's own custom macros — same name(...)-call ambiguity #functions has. Known names (the same ~214-name list as #knownCommandsInProse) get support.function.tf — tf provides these, same family as a known #functions call. Anything else (presumably your own macro) gets entity.name.function.tf — a name being invoked that this engine can't confirm is built-in, same standard support.*-vs-entity.name.*-for-user-defined convention real grammars use (confirmed in VS Code's own bundled bash grammar). /@word is the same command either way, just forced to resolve to the real builtin even if a same-named macro exists to shadow it (htmldoc/topics/macros.html: "If a macro and builtin have the same name, the macro will be called. Typing '/@' ... will always call the builtin command.") — stdlib.tf leans on this throughout (/@test, /@eval, /@list, ...). The @ always gets keyword.operator.tf regardless of which branch the name falls in.

patterns.comment: Known branch: tried first, so an exact match here wins over the unrecognized fallback below.
Unrecognized branch: anything else shaped like /word — presumably your own macro.
